newsitem.title: UK: World wheat demand to rise 3-6 mln T in 97/98 - AWB.
newsitem.headline: World wheat demand to rise 3-6 mln T in 97/98 - AWB.

text.p: World wheat demand will rise by some three to six million tonnes in 1997-98 with most of the rise coming from Iran, Iraq, Turkey, India and Pakistan, according to Australian Wheat Board estimates.
World stocks will fall by up to six million tonnes, AWB chairman Trevor Flugge said in a speech to the International Grains Council's annual conference in London on Friday.

According to latest IGC estimates published on June 5, world wheat trade will rise to 93 million tonnes in 1997-98 from 91 million in 96-97 and stocks will fall to 96 million tonnes in 1997-98 from 100 million.

Flugge said the key to calculating import demand lay in Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and India. "In 1996-97 these five markets doubled their imports from around seven million tonnes to 14 million tonnes," he said.

"The AWB believes that these same five markets will have an even stronger import requirement in 1997-98, with imports likely to increase a further 4.0 to 4.5 million tonnes to 18.5 million tonnes," he said.

Drought in parts of Africa will also lead to increased import needs and demand in Asia, particularly Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh was also forecast higher. This meant total demand would outstrip growth in supply, leading to a fall in world stocks, particularly in exporters such as Canada and the EU.
"As such we believe there is no justification for the use of export subsidies in 1997-98," he said.
Flugge put US wheat acreage some eight percent down at about 28 million hectares. Canada's wheat acreage is seen falling by 10 percent to some 11.5 million hectares.
He estimated EU wheat acreage three percent up at about 17 million hectares.

Australia's area is likely to be 0.5 percent lower at 11.1 million hectares while Argentina's is estimated seven percent down at 5.7 million hectares. Production was heavily predicated on reasonable growing conditions over the coming months.

"The presence of El Nino was confirmed by Australia's Bureau of Meteorology on the third of June, indicating that drier than average conditions will persist for the next 12 to 15 months," Flugge said.
But he pointed out El Nino would only affect a small part of Australia. Rains had been very favourable in Western Australia, Queensland and much of New South Wales.
"As a result stored soil moistures reserves, the result of plentiful rainfall during the February-April period, are very favourable in these states," he said.
These represent 70 percent of Australia's wheat production, Flugge said. --Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 7928
